Photograph: Peter Lopeman/Alamy View image in fullscreen While the UK bucked the trend, results on the continent continued a slide that began in 2018. Photograph: Peter Lopeman/Alamy Education European education powerhouses rocked by falling scores in global study France and Germany among countries with low Pisa scores, which show how well 15-year-olds use school learning in life Jon Henley , Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angelique Chrisafis in Paris and Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F rance’s were its worst ever. Germany’s, too. In the Netherlands, results also tumbled to all-time lows. Even in Finland, Europe’s much-vaunted schools champion and a global leader for decades, scores plummeted. The 2025 Pisa scores, which assess how effectively 15-year-olds apply school-learned knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations, have rocked some of western Europe’s education powerhouses. While the UK bucked the trend , results on the continent continued a slide that began in 2018. In France, Germany, the Netherlands and Finland, the proportion of 15-year-olds lacking basic functional literacy and maths skills rose to nearly one in three. Pandemic learning losses accelerated the drop, but education experts say the roots of the problem run much deeper: chronic teacher shortages, repeated curriculum reforms that have neglected basic skills and widening inequalities within increasingly segregated systems. Compounding it all, incessant smartphone use has dramatically reduced attention spans, replacing “deep reading” with scrolling, and pupil motivation has collapsed. Pupils in Germany got their worst-ever Pisa report card, reviving a decades-old debate about the country’s weaknesses in schools, integration and closing the wealth gap. Samuel Greiff, the German Pisa study coordinator, noted an alarming rise in youngsters who lack basic skills for citizenship and employment, including the ability to understand a written text and do rudimentary consumer maths. The study found that in Europe’s top economy the link between academic performance and socioeconomic status was particularly strong: only 2% of pupils from low-income families achieve high levels of competence, against 25% from higher-income families – a correlation twice as strong as in Denmark or Norway. “Other countries are far more successful in decoupling educational success from family background,” Greiff told local media, noting that class had a far greater influence on teens’ academic success than whether their family had immigrated. Germany endured a first “Pisa-Schock” in 2000, when the report’s dismal ratings triggered a nationwide effort to raise performance. The 2012 report identified significant improvement, putting the country above the OECD average. But the 2025 edition showed Germany slipping back to average, with about one in four pupils lacking competency in natural sciences and one in three in reading and maths. About one in five demonstrated insufficient capabilities in all three areas. The number of teens deemed “at risk” because they lacked the reading and maths skills for further education has doubled over the last decade, and reading for pleasure has declined at a faster rate in Germany than in other industrialised countries: one in two 15-year-olds said they only read when it was required. . Strikingly, pupils from the most socioeconomically privileged neighbourhoods recorded the sharpest decline in reading comprehension. Education minister Karin Prien said the report required an urgent response, highlighting the negative influence of excessive social media use and pledging to present new measures to protect younger children by the end of the year. In the Netherlands, the scores marked a historic low point, setting troubling new records in reading literacy, where a record 39% of 15-year-olds now lack the basic skills required to navigate modern society, evaluate the credibility of sources or process multi-page texts, up from 33% in the previous 2022 edition. Researchers noted that the Dutch reading score has plunged by more than 60 points over the last decade, meaning today’s 15-year-olds are effectively reading at the level that 12-year-olds achieved 10 years ago. The decline was less marked in maths, where Dutch pupils once dominated the European rankings, but still represented a record low only marginally higher than the OECD average, while the science score was also below its previous level. . The Dutch education ministry promised urgent action, acknowledging that the assessment “confirms our decline was not a temporary post-pandemic dip, but a structural issue. We can’t accept a society where a third of our youth leave school unprepared for basic reading in daily life.” However, teachers’ unions and literacy advocates reacted with frustration. The AOb teachers’ union argued reading levels would never improve as long as “classes are routinely cancelled, non-qualified staff are filling gaps, and the workload is driving experienced educators out of the profession.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The reading advocacy group Stichting Lezen added that the failure lay “not with pupils, but with an approach that has turned reading into a set of mechanical comprehension tricks rather than fostering deep reading habits”. In France, the scores were similarly grim. “It’s worrying, but it’s unfortunately not a surprise,” said Édouard Geffray, the education minister. Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, called the outcome a “catastrophe” and a reflection of the nation’s decline. French education analysts have long warned of a lack of state investment, particularly in primary schools, as well as a highly unequal system where socioeconomic status dictates results, while governments have tended to approach education failings by debating timetabling and how many hours children sit at their desks. Over the past decade, a succession of eight different education ministers has resulted in constant policy changes and reversals, leaving teachers feeling more stressed by the avalanche of directives than by teaching in class. Mid-career salaries, meanwhile, remain below the OECD average and another recent report found just 4% of French teachers felt valued . Éric Charbonnier, an OECD education analyst, argued that the focus should shift away from debates over desk hours toward greater autonomy to explore teaching methods, and more method-focused training. In Finland, average results were lower than in 2022 in maths and reading, and stable in science. Dr Arto K Ahonen, Pisa national project manager at the Finnish Institute for Educational Research, said the results had prompted serious discussion over pupils’ perseverance and effort. . “The goal remains to reverse the decline and return to a rising trend,” Ahonen said. “Meanwhile, we recognise the universal decline we are part of.” Ahonen noted that the Finnish system had seen “no major change in our education system in 50 years,” warning that “curricula must be renewed as times and society change. It’s unlikely that any school system could operate with the same curricula for decades, even a successful one.” In neighbouring Sweden, record-low results spurred heated political debate ahead of recent elections, with party leaders blaming everything from screens to immigration and insufficient teaching staff. But experts say there is no single explanation. In its report on the latest scores, Skolverket, the national education agency, said several changes were already under way aimed at reinforcing pupils’ knowledge and the classroom role of teachers in creating a “safer and more equal environment”. Composite: Guardian Design/AP/Reuters/Getty Images/Sopa Images/Rex/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen The Trump administration is deporting people to countries where they often have no connections. Composite: Guardian Design/AP/Reuters/Getty Images/Sopa Images/Rex/Shutterstock First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Banished to alien lands – Trump’s secret deportation deals Thousands of people deported from the US to countries where they have no connections. Plus, European spy chiefs warn of Moscow action against Nato Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Jem Bartholomew Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.33 BST Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.12 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands of people deported from the US on the back of shadowy deals made with dozens of countries. Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US, intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead. The Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Forbidden Stories. The consortium reviewed documents and interviewed more than 100 people on the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration. At what scale are third-country deportations happening? Since returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has deported more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own. Which countries are people being deported to? The Trump administration has struck 35 deals allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to countries where they often have no connections. Is this legal? A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration’s third-country removals policy was unlawful. A three-judge panel unanimously agreed that it violated due process. But the government has 90 days to appeal against the court’s decision, and is expected to do so. European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato View image in fullscreen There are fears Vladimir Putin’s regime is making preparations for more decisive action in Europe. Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”, the Guardian’s Shaun Walker reports . The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months. The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. How imminent is the threat? Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy. “It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said. Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh after missile and drone strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saturday. Photograph: Reuters Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against it. Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”. What has Iran said? The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack did take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”. What has caused the outburst of sabre-rattling? It appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force. In other news … View image in fullscreen Friedrich Merz is facing growing calls to quit. Photograph: Hannibal Hanschke/EPA Friedrich Merz, Germany’s chancellor, has vowed to stay in office, despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party. Gavin Newsom, the California governor, has signed off on a package of bills aimed at bolstering election security, including measures to block federal political interference. Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the assassination of the Haitian president, Jovenel Moïse , who was killed in July 2021, according to US officials. Starbucks workers say their health insurance premiums have soared this year, in some cases more than doubling, according to a survey conducted by Starbucks Workers United. Stat of the day: 2.7m more lives could be saved in next pandemic if vaccines are shared more fairly, says report View image in fullscreen Fast-tracking vaccine development could massively cut death rates, say scientists. Photograph: Jacob King/PA An extra 2.7 million lives could be saved in the next pandemic if countries share vaccines in a less selfish way, a new study has found – although the death toll in richer countries would rise. Researchers modelling a hypothetical global outbreak of flu found that fast-tracking vaccine development could cut deaths from 58.5m to 23.9m. Building Power: They fought against datacenters. Now they are running for local offices View image in fullscreen A protest against a planned datacenter in the Ellenwood neighborhood of Decatur, Georgia. Photograph: Erik S Lesser/EPA A national datacenter revolt – which has built coalitions between environmentalists and Nimbys, conservatives and democratic socialists – is turning some community organizers into political hopefuls, Claire Wang writes . Dozens of datacenter activists are running for offices held by incumbents that they feel have disregarded issues of affordability, environment destructive and the overreach of tech power. Don’t miss this: Is culture alive? View image in fullscreen ‘Language is not only a fundamental part of culture; it’s also our most powerful means of transmitting cultural information.’ Illustration: Elia Barbieri “Cultural traditions endure because they share a fundamental property with biological organisms. They are alive. Not metaphorically, but literally,” writes Jonathan Loh for the big idea . “I believe that human culture isn’t just an accidental add-on to organic life; rather, it’s a separate expression of life in its own right.” Climate check: EPA let Bayer pick regulations for destructive weedkiller, documents show View image in fullscreen Soybean crops in Sioux County, Iowa, this month. Photograph: Jerry Mennenga/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock The Environmental Protection Agency allowed Bayer to pick from a menu of regulation options for the controversial and destructive weedkiller dicamba, internal agency documents reveal – then it put Bayer’s choices into a proposed federal rule. The Center for Biological Diversity has brought a lawsuit over the issue. Last Thing: ‘I got married in it’ – Guardian readers on their favorite thrifted fashion finds View image in fullscreen Alicia wore a $5 dress on her wedding day. Photograph: Alicia The anti-poverty charity Oxfam is challenging people to avoid buying new clothes for 30 days and choose preloved pieces instead. The Guardian asked readers about their best thrifted finds . “From a distance it looks pink, but as you get closer you realise it’s swirls of pink dots creating an optical illusion,” Alicia said, of her $5 wedding dress. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/30/moro.text: Morocco's King Mohammed VI named Urban Planning Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country's prime minister on Tuesday, making the 50-year-old attorney the first woman to hold the office in the Muslim kingdom.Mansouri, who until her nomination also was the mayor of Marrakech, was tasked with forming a new government, the Royal Palace said in a statement. The announcement came four days after results of parliamentary elections were announced, with Mansouri’s centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, scoring the highest votes.Mansouri, the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Najla Bouden in Tunisia, is expected to build a coalition in the coming days to form a government. Morocco’s electoral system makes it difficult for a single party to win an absolute majority.Her government is expected to make billions of dollars in investments linked to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, while seeking to deliver on promises to fight inflation, raise wages and create jobs.The Moroccan Constitution gives the king, who is the country’s highest authority, the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections.That was a change successfully pushed by Arab Spring protesters in 2011. Before that, the king could name the prime minister without any such restriction.Mansouri joined PAM upon its creation in 2008 by Fouad Ali el-Himma, a childhood friend and close adviser to the king.A law graduate from the University of Montpellier in France, Mansouri became one of the party’s top leaders in 2024. She twice served as mayor of Marrakech and was a member of parliament.Mansouri is the daughter of the “pasha of Marrakech” Abderrahmane el-Mansouri, a senior local official who was also Morocco’s ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, headed Marrakech’s bar association and was a major landowner.She faced accusations of conflict of interest after a group of unidentified hackers claimed she had used her position for personal gain regarding land transactions in Marrakech. Mansouri denied the allegations, called them defamatory and took legal action.One million of the 15.8 million registered voters in last week’s election voted for the Authenticity and Modernity Party, marking its first win since its creation. The election was the first since the Ceuta migration crisis last July and deadly youth-led protests last year.After the royal nomination, the focus shifts to the coalition that will form the next government.PAM has expressed its willingness to work with all parties, but some, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have announced no plans of such collaboration, insisting they will remain in the opposition.
